newsitem.title: CUBA: Cubans flock to attend Saint Lazarus pilgrimage.
newsitem.headline: Cubans flock to attend Saint Lazarus pilgrimage.

text.p: Thousands of Cubans, many crawling on their knees or stomachs, flocked on Tuesday to a shrine outside Havana in an annual pilgrimage to Saint Lazarus that combines Catholicism with more exotic Afro-Cuban beliefs.

The number of people taking part in the island's traditional San Lazaro pilgrimage has visibly increased in the last few years as Cuba's communist authorities have shown increased tolerance towards religious activities.

This year's event was given added interest by the prospect of a visit to Cuba next year by Pope John Paul II following a historic meeting with Cuban President Fidel Castro at the Vatican last month. One preacher speaking on Monday night at the San Lazaro shrine on the outskirts of Havana urged worshippers to prepare spiritually for the papal visit.

Following tradition, devotees of Saint Lazarus, worshipped as the deity Babalu-Aye in the parallel Afro-Cuban religion of "santeria," carried out various forms of public penitence to honour pledges made to the saint.

In the most common form, worshippers crawled to the shrine on their hands and knees. Others carried crosses or children on their shoulders or, in more elaborate diplays, dressed in sackcloth and dragged heavy weights chained to their bodies.
In both Catholicism and "santeria", Saint Lazarus or Babalu-Aye is associated with sickness and healing.

Ragged beggars displaying effigies of the saint lined the door to the San Lazaro church -- begging is also considered a form of worship. Inside the candle-lit church, flowers were heaped on altars while offerings of coins and banknotes were collected by church workers.
Many worshippers sipped rum and puffed cigars, both used for ritual cleansings in "santeria."

The San Lazaro pilgrimage is a rare public outpouring of religious fervor in a country whose one-party constitution declares socialism the official ideology. Uniformed and plain-clothes police were deployed along the pilgrimage route and around the shrine to prevent disturbances.

Cuban Catholic Church leaders say they do not encourage the idol worship and non-orthodox Afro-Cuban beliefs associated with "santeria" but they recognise these have a strong following among Cuba's 11 million people.

The pilgrimage, which lasts several days, also provided a business bonanza for dozens of improvised private cafes and restaurants set up along the route serving drinks, plantain fritters, roast pork and other traditional Cuban food.
